query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys resist combined wear and corrosion by rapidly reforming a complex, multi-element oxide film when the protective layer is disrupted by mechanical abrasion. This self-healing passivation, driven by high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion, keeps the overall degradation lower than the simple additive effects of wear and corrosion observed in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-synthesized, multi-principal element HEA (e.g., an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi composition) with a high density of defects and severe lattice distortion that favors the formation of multi-component oxide films.
generation.intervention: Subject both the HEA and a matched baseline alloy (with similar bulk mechanical properties but lacking the high-entropy driven oxide reformation capability) to cyclic mechanical abrasion in a chloride-rich corrosive electrolyte.
generation.conditions: Cyclic abrasion combined with immersion in a chloride-rich solution at controlled temperatures that allow for adequate oxidation kinetics. The test should include isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and combined (simultaneous wear and corrosion) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A rapidly reforming, multi-element oxide film at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the protective oxide layer; however, in the HEA the high entropy and lattice distortions promote fast reformation of a multi-component oxide film. This dynamic self-healing process reduces the overall damage by preventing the additive effects of wear and corrosion from fully developing.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined degradation conditions, the HEA will show a total degradation rate that is lower than the sum of the individual rates measured under isolated wear and isolated corrosion. Conversely, the baseline alloy is expected to exhibit degradation rates that approach or exceed the additive sum of its isolated modes.
generation.baseline: A conventional alloy with comparable bulk mechanical properties but a simpler elemental composition that does not support rapid, multi-component oxide reformation.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold in environments that enable prompt oxide film formation (e.g., sufficiently high temperature and oxygen availability) but may fail in settings with suppressed oxidation kinetics (e.g., very low temperatures or inert atmospheres).
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend of dynamic passivation is supported, the exact kinetics of oxide reformation and the quantitative magnitude of the reduction in combined degradation remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a cyclic abrasion test in a chloride-rich electrolyte on both the HEA and the baseline alloy. Vary temperature to adjust oxide reformation kinetics. For each sample, perform isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and combined wear-corrosion tests while monitoring the surface for oxide film reformation.
measurements: Wear track volume loss (using interferometric scanning)
Electrochemical corrosion rates (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and linear polarization)
Surface oxide film characteristics (thickness and continuity via SEM/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, under combined degradation conditions, the HEA exhibits a degradation rate equal to or greater than the sum of its isolated wear and corrosion rates, or if no evidence of rapid oxide film reformation is observed following mechanical disruption.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), a novel class of multi-principal element alloys, brought a new era in the study of alloy materials []. The presence of five or more elements in close proximity to the iso-atomic ratio endows alloys with high configurational entropy, which confers upon HEAs the capacity to form stable simple solid solution phases. This, in turn, endows HEAs with exceptional mechanical properties and commendable corrosion resistance []. This property gives high-entropy alloys excellent mechanical and physical properties, including high strength, high fracture toughness, and the ability to conduct electricity at very low temperatures []. In addition, they exhibit excellent resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Consequently, in the aerospace field [], where the temperature of service varies widely, in the field of ultra-high temperature structural materials [], in marine industrial equipment [], and in the nuclear industry [], where there are harsh working conditions, high-entropy alloys have a wider range of application prospects than traditional alloys due to their rich elemental composition and flexible selection of elemental content. The oxide layer formed on the Al-HEA coating had different composition and structure in comparison with the Mo-HEA oxide layer after the aerated test. The oxide layer on Al-HEA coating was found to have more corrosion damage characteristics rather than passive layer behavior, i.e., not with compact structure. The Al-HEA oxide layer was in some cases detached from the bulk material, and the layer was composed of oxides from all the elements in the HEA as seen in Figure 10. In addition, localized corrosion damage enriched in Al-O was also observed on the surface of the Al-HEA coating in locations where the complex oxide film had not formed to a significant extent as seen in Figure 11. Localized oxide corrosion forms were observed in the aerated test but not in the wellhead test. The Al-O-rich localized damage might suggest that the oxidation of Al has faster kinetics than the oxidation of the other elements. This localized corrosion behavior also strengthens the assumption that the complex oxide film is not passive. Cracks were also observed in the Al-HEA coating in the sample Al-HEA-304L after the exposure in the aerated environment as seen in Figure 12.

frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) fabricated in their as-synthesized, multi-principal element state, intended for use in environments that combine aggressive chemical (corrosive) attack with mechanical wear.
frame.goal: Develop a unified, single mechanistic hypothesis that explains resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion by defining the interdependence between mechanical disruption and protective passivation behavior, and predict the performance difference compared to a matched baseline alloy.
frame.limitation: Existing studies typically address wear and corrosion separately; there is a gap in a holistic understanding that couples the effects of mechanical damage (which disrupts protective surface films) and the alloy’s intrinsic ability to reform passivating layers under corrosive conditions.
root_cause_cues: governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion
constraints: Must provide a single mechanistic hypothesis that couples both degradation modes
The hypothesis should be testable via a controlled comparison (i.e. an experiment with a matched baseline)
Comparisons must account for both separate and combined effects of wear and corrosion
frame.regime: Environments combining aggressive chemical attack (e.g., chloride-rich solutions) with mechanical abrasion or sliding contact, such that the protective passivating film on the alloy is intermittently disrupted.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have separately optimized HEAs for high wear resistance (e.g., via high hardness and toughness) and for corrosion resistance (via passive film stability).
These studies fell short in addressing the interdependence of mechanical and chemical degradation, often neglecting the dynamic behavior of passivation under wear-induced film breakdown.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis is that the simultaneous degradation resistance of HEAs arises from a self-regenerating passivation mechanism that is intrinsically coupled to the alloy’s high defect density and severe lattice distortion. Under mechanical wear, the disrupted passivating surface rapidly reforms due to the high entropy-driven thermodynamic stability of multi-element oxide layers, thus continuously protecting the underlying metal. This dynamic recovery process is what governs resistance to concurrent wear and corrosion.
frame.method: A proposed controlled comparison would involve testing HEA samples versus a baseline alloy (with similar bulk properties but without the high entropy effect) under identical conditions: subjecting both to cyclic mechanical abrasion combined with immersion in a corrosive medium. Measurements should separately quantify the rates of wear (material loss via abrasion) and corrosion (electrochemical degradation) as well as combined synergistic effects. The prediction is that, in the HEA, the rate of combined degradation will be lower than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion rates observed under isolated conditions, signifying an active self-healing of the passive film. The hypothesis should hold under conditions where the chemical environment allows for rapid oxide formation but may fail under conditions where the oxidation kinetics are too slow (e.g., low temperature or inert environments). Prior evidence would include studies on passivation kinetics in multi-component alloys and observations of self-healing behavior in high entropy systems. An observation that would falsify the hypothesis is if under combined wear and corrosion conditions the HEA exhibits accelerated degradation compared to either mode in isolation, or if no recovery of the passive film is observed despite clear mechanical disruption.

decision.trend: Early research on HEAs focused on optimizing individual degradation modes—mechanical properties such as high hardness, strength, and wear resistance on one side and corrosion resistance through stable passive films on the other. Studies like those in PMC7866258 and PMC11857682 demonstrated that HEAs can exhibit both excellent wear resistance and good corrosion performance, but they treated these modes separately. Over time, researchers began to note that the high defect densities and lattice distortions intrinsic to multi-principal element alloys might foster dynamic oxide reformation. However, despite hints in passivation kinetics and microstructural evidence, no study has yet demonstrated a unified, mechanistically coupled self-healing response under simultaneous wear and corrosive attack.
decision.unsolved: The core unresolved issue is whether the high-entropy effect can drive a self-regenerating passive film in situ when the protective layer is continuously disrupted by mechanical wear. No previous work has quantitatively linked the rapid reformation of a multi-element oxide layer to a measurable reduction in the combined degradation rate versus the sum of its isolated wear and corrosion contributions.
decision.lever: Perform a cyclic abrasion test in a chloride-rich electrolyte with in situ electrochemical monitoring. Specifically, test an HEA sample against a baseline alloy of comparable bulk mechanical properties but lacking the multi-element configuration. Key parameters include modulating the electrolyte temperature to vary the oxide reformation kinetics and comparing degradation rates under isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and combined conditions.
decision.why: This experiment directly targets the hypothesis that high-entropy alloys exhibit a self-healing passivation mechanism that mitigates simultaneous degradation. It follows the trend of moving from isolated property optimization towards integrated testing and is designed to reveal whether the dynamic recovery of the passive film under cyclic mechanical disruption is sufficient to reduce the overall damage compared to the additive sum of individual effects. The controlled variable approach, with environmental modulation to test the limits, aligns with both the research gap and the cues from prior studies.
